claim: Natural killer (NK) cells play a crucial role in immunity, killing virally infected and cancerous cells.
source: Natural killer (NK) cells play a crucial role in immunity, killing virally infected and cancerous cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about NK cell function in the immune system.

claim: The balance of signals initiated upon engagement of activating and inhibitory NK receptors with cognate ligands determines killing or tolerance.
source: The balance of signals initiated upon engagement of activating and inhibitory NK receptors with cognate ligands determines killing or tolerance.
evidence: This represents established understanding of NK cell regulation cited in the introduction.

claim: The SHP-1 tyrosine phosphatase is the central negative NK cell regulator that dephosphorylates key activating signaling proteins.
source: The SHP-1 tyrosine phosphatase is the central negative NK cell regulator that dephosphorylates key activating signaling proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SHP-1 function in NK cells.

claim: Phosphorylation of SHP-1 in NK cells on the S591 residue by PKC-θ promotes the inhibited SHP-1 'folded' state.
source: Here, we show that phosphorylation of SHP-1 in NK cells on the S591 residue by PKC-θ promotes the inhibited SHP-1 'folded' state.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data including FRET analysis and biochemical assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: Silencing PKC-θ maintains SHP-1 in the active conformation.
source: Silencing PKC-θ maintains SHP-1 in the active conformation, reduces NK cell activation and cytotoxicity, and promotes tumor progression in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by FRET efficiency measurements shown in Figure 5 and PTP activity assays.

claim: Silencing PKC-θ reduces NK cell activation and cytotoxicity.
source: Silencing PKC-θ maintains SHP-1 in the active conformation, reduces NK cell activation and cytotoxicity, and promotes tumor progression in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by calcium flux measurements, cytotoxicity assays, and degranulation assays shown in Figure 7.

claim: Silencing PKC-θ promotes tumor progression in vivo.
source: Silencing PKC-θ maintains SHP-1 in the active conformation, reduces NK cell activation and cytotoxicity, and promotes tumor progression in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by xenograft mouse model data shown in Figure 8.

claim: NK cells release cytotoxic granules containing perforin and Granzyme B, which induce target cell death.
source: NK cell effector functions are carried out by the release of cytotoxic granules containing perforin and Granzyme B, which induce target cell death (Pipkin and Lieberman, 2007; Topham and Hewitt, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NK cells produce cytokines and chemokines, such as IFN-γ, which activate the adaptive immune response.
source: Furthermore, NK cells produce cytokines and chemokines, such as IFN-γ, which activate the adaptive immune response (Malhotra and Shanker, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Activation or inhibition of NK function depends on the balance between signals derived from activating and inhibitory receptors on the NK cell surface.
source: Activation or inhibition of NK function was shown to depend on the balance between signals derived from activating and inhibitory receptors on the NK cell surface (Lanier, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) are found on cytoplasmic tails of the transmembrane adaptor proteins CD3ζ, FcɛRIγ, and DAP12.
source: These include immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) found on cytoplasmic tails of the transmembrane adaptor proteins CD3ζ, FcɛRIγ, and DAP12, or the YINM motif on the DAP10 adaptor, which associates with the NKG2D receptor (André et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The YINM motif on the DAP10 adaptor associates with the NKG2D receptor.
source: These include immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) found on cytoplasmic tails of the transmembrane adaptor proteins CD3ζ, FcɛRIγ, and DAP12, or the YINM motif on the DAP10 adaptor, which associates with the NKG2D receptor (André et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Immunoreceptor tyrosine-based switch motifs (ITSMs) are found on the CD244 receptor.
source: Another group of motifs includes the immunoreceptor tyrosine-based switch motifs (ITSMs) on the CD244 receptor (Vyas et al., 2002b; Lanier, 2003; Feng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibitory NK cell receptors express immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibition motifs (ITIMs) on their cytoplasmic tails.
source: Inhibitory NK cell receptors express a separate target sequence for signal suppression, consisting of immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibition motifs (ITIMs) expressed on the cytoplasmic tails (Long, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The key receptors facilitating NK inhibition recognize major histocompatibility class 1 (MHC-I) molecules expressed on the majority of cells in the body.
source: The key receptors facilitating NK inhibition recognize major histocompatibility class 1 (MHC-I) molecules expressed on the majority of cells in the body.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NK cell inhibitory receptors.

claim: The killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor (KIR) family is expressed in humans and primates.
source: These receptors include the killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor (KIR) family in humans and primates, the Ly49 family in mice, and NKG2A/CD94 receptors expressed in both primates and mice (Orr and Lanier, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The Ly49 family of receptors is expressed in mice.
source: These receptors include the killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor (KIR) family in humans and primates, the Ly49 family in mice, and NKG2A/CD94 receptors expressed in both primates and mice (Orr and Lanier, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NKG2A/CD94 receptors are expressed in both primates and mice.
source: These receptors include the killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor (KIR) family in humans and primates, the Ly49 family in mice, and NKG2A/CD94 receptors expressed in both primates and mice (Orr and Lanier, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NGK2A/CD94 receptors have specificity for the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) isoform E (HLA-E).
source: NGK2A/CD94 were shown to have specificity for the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) isoform E (HLA-E), whereas the KIR family of inhibitory receptors was shown to associate with HLA-C and HLA-B (Moretta et al., 1994; Wagtmann et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The KIR family of inhibitory receptors associates with HLA-C and HLA-B.
source: NGK2A/CD94 were shown to have specificity for the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) isoform E (HLA-E), whereas the KIR family of inhibitory receptors was shown to associate with HLA-C and HLA-B (Moretta et al., 1994; Wagtmann et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Engagement of inhibitory receptors with their cognate ligands and phosphorylation of their ITIM motifs recruits SHP-1.
source: Engagement of these receptors with their cognate ligands and phosphorylation of their ITIM motifs recruits the Src-homology 2-domain (SH2)-containing protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP), SHP-1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SHP-1 recruitment mechanism.

claim: SHP-1 dephosphorylates key proteins involved in the activating signaling pathway, thereby downregulating NK cell activation.
source: SHP-1 consequently dephosphorylates key proteins involved in the activating signaling pathway, thereby downregulating NK cell activation (Stebbins et al., 2003; Matalon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SHP-1 comprises a catalytic phosphatase domain near its C′ terminus.
source: SHP-1 comprises a catalytic phosphatase domain near its C′ terminus, two phospho-tyrosine binding SH2 domains toward its N′ terminus, and sites of tyrosine and serine phosphorylation at the end of its C′-terminal tail (Lorenz, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature describing SHP-1 structure.

claim: SHP-1 has two phospho-tyrosine binding SH2 domains toward its N′ terminus.
source: SHP-1 comprises a catalytic phosphatase domain near its C′ terminus, two phospho-tyrosine binding SH2 domains toward its N′ terminus, and sites of tyrosine and serine phosphorylation at the end of its C′-terminal tail (Lorenz, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature describing SHP-1 structure.

claim: SHP-1 has sites of tyrosine and serine phosphorylation at the end of its C′-terminal tail.
source: SHP-1 comprises a catalytic phosphatase domain near its C′ terminus, two phospho-tyrosine binding SH2 domains toward its N′ terminus, and sites of tyrosine and serine phosphorylation at the end of its C′-terminal tail (Lorenz, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature describing SHP-1 structure.

claim: In its autoinhibited closed state, the SHP-1 N′ SH2 domain associates with the catalytic domain, blocking access to its substrates.
source: In its autoinhibited closed state, the SHP-1 N′ SH2 domain associates with the catalytic domain, blocking access to its substrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SHP-1 autoinhibition mechanism.

claim: Binding of SHP-1 SH2 domains to phosphorylated tyrosine residues on the ITIM of the inhibitory receptors induces a conformational alteration in SHP-1.
source: Binding of SHP-1 SH2 domains to phosphorylated tyrosine residues on the ITIM of the inhibitory receptors induces a conformational alteration in SHP-1. This releases it from the inhibited state and enables its catalytic activity, that is, dephosphorylation of key signaling molecules and inhibition of NK cell function (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SHP-1 substrates in NK cells include the guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF), VAV1.
source: SHP-1 substrates in NK cells include the guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF), VAV1 (Stebbins et al., 2003), phospholipase C gamma 1/2 (PLCγ1/2), and linker for activation of T cells (LAT), recently identified by our group (Matalon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SHP-1 substrates in NK cells include phospholipase C gamma 1/2 (PLCγ1/2).
source: SHP-1 substrates in NK cells include the guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF), VAV1 (Stebbins et al., 2003), phospholipase C gamma 1/2 (PLCγ1/2), and linker for activation of T cells (LAT), recently identified by our group (Matalon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature from the authors' group.

claim: SHP-1 substrates in NK cells include linker for activation of T cells (LAT).
source: SHP-1 substrates in NK cells include the guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF), VAV1 (Stebbins et al., 2003), phospholipase C gamma 1/2 (PLCγ1/2), and linker for activation of T cells (LAT), recently identified by our group (Matalon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature from the authors' group.

claim: Cancer cells can upregulate ligands for inhibitory NK receptors such as HLA-E and PD-L1 to repress NK cell activity through SHP-1 recruitment and activity.
source: Therefore, upregulation of ligands for inhibitory NK receptors that express ITIMs by cancer cells, such as HLA-E and PD-L1, may repress NK cell activity through SHP-1 recruitment and activity (Carretero et al., 1998; Chemnitz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and represents inference about cancer immune evasion.

claim: Actin retrograde flow (ARF) induces a physical conformational change in the SHP-1 molecule to facilitate its activity.
source: We recently revealed that actin retrograde flow (ARF) induces a physical conformational change in the SHP-1 molecule to facilitate its activity (Matalon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work from the authors' group.

claim: SHP-1 localizes to the lytic NK cell immunological synapse (NKIS).
source: SHP-1 was shown to localize to the lytic NK cell immunological synapse (NKIS) (Vyas et al., 2002a), yet the mechanism by which its activity at the lytic synapse is regulated was not determined.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SHP-1 in NK cells is heavily phosphorylated on the serine 591 residue (S591) via Protein kinase c theta (PKC-θ) during activating but not inhibitory responses, within the first 5 min of NK cell activation.
source: Here, we demonstrate that in NK cells SHP-1 is heavily phosphorylated on the serine 591 residue (S591) via Protein kinase c theta (PKC-θ) (and hence dormant) during activating but not inhibitory responses, within the first 5 min of NK cell activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: SHP-1 phosphorylation is dynamic and increases along the progression of the inhibitory NKIS.
source: This phosphorylation is dynamic and increases along the progression of the inhibitory NKIS, while slightly decreasing during progression of the activating NKIS.
evidence: This is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SHP-1 phosphorylation slightly decreases during progression of the activating NKIS.
source: This phosphorylation is dynamic and increases along the progression of the inhibitory NKIS, while slightly decreasing during progression of the activating NKIS.
evidence: This is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SHP-1 phosphorylation dynamics are closely correlated with changes in SHP-1 catalytic conformations.
source: SHP-1 phosphorylation dynamics were also closely correlated with changes in SHP-1 catalytic conformations.
evidence: This is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 2 correlating with phosphorylation data in Figure 1.

claim: Blocking PKC-θ-mediated phosphorylation of SHP-1 restored SHP-1 activity and inhibited NK cell activation.
source: Blocking PKC-θ-mediated phosphorylation of SHP-1 restored SHP-1 activity and inhibited NK cell activation.
evidence: This is supported by PKC-θ silencing experiments shown in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: NK cells bearing a phosphor-mimetic point mutation that suppresses SHP-1 activity at the serine 591 residue were highly activated.
source: Furthermore, NK cells bearing a phosphor-mimetic point mutation that suppresses SHP-1 activity 1 at the serine 591 residue were highly activated.
evidence: This is supported by data from SHP-1 S591D mutant cells shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Knockout of SHP-1 in NK cells rescued PKC-θ silencing and promoted tumor clearance in vivo.
source: Finally, knockout of SHP-1 in NK cells rescued PKC-θ silencing and promoted tumor clearance in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in Figure 8.

claim: High S591 phosphorylation levels occur during activating interactions after 5 min of incubation.
source: Our data revealed different SHP-1 phosphorylation profiles during NK cell inhibition and activation after 5 min of incubation (Figure 1A). High S591 phosphorylation levels could be seen during activating interactions (3.06 ± 0.31, p=0.0104), whereas lower SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation was observed during induced inhibitory interactions.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data and quantification shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Lower SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation is observed during induced inhibitory interactions after 5 min of incubation.
source: Our data revealed different SHP-1 phosphorylation profiles during NK cell inhibition and activation after 5 min of incubation (Figure 1A). High S591 phosphorylation levels could be seen during activating interactions (3.06 ± 0.31, p=0.0104), whereas lower SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation was observed during induced inhibitory interactions.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data and quantification shown in Figure 1A.

claim: pNK-2DL1 cells incubated with activating 721-HLA-negative cells show higher SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation compared to cells incubated with inhibiting 721-Cw4 targets (2.51 ± 0.19, p=0.006).
source: The same pattern was observed during incubation of pNK-2DL1 cells with activating 721-HLA-negative cells or with inhibiting 721-Cw4 targets cells (2.51 ± 0.19, p=0.006, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data and quantification shown in Figure 1B.

claim: pS591 on SHP-1 was dramatically altered during formation of the inhibitory NKIS, showing almost no initial phosphorylation after 5 min of incubation, and displaying high phosphorylation by 20 min.
source: Strikingly, we found that pS591 on SHP-1 was dramatically altered during formation of the inhibitory NKIS, showing almost no initial phosphorylation after 5 min of incubation, and displaying high phosphorylation by 20 min.
evidence: This is supported by time-course immunoblot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Activating NK cell interactions displayed higher SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation during the first 5 min of activation, remaining relatively stable, with a slight (nonsignificant) reduction after 20 min of activation.
source: Activating NK cell interactions, however, displayed higher SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation during the first 5 min of activation, remaining relatively stable, with a slight (nonsignificant) reduction after 20 min of activation (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-course immunoblot data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: SHP-1 activation status is correlated with its conformation.
source: It is known that SHP-1 activation status is correlated with its conformation (Poole and Jones, 2005; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the closed conformation, the N′ SH2 domain masks the catalytic domain rendering the enzyme inactive.
source: In the closed conformation, the N′ SH2 domain masks the catalytic domain rendering the enzyme inactive, whereas when the catalytic domain is free of the N′ SH2 domain, the protein remains in an open active conformation (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: When the catalytic domain is free of the N′ SH2 domain, the protein remains in an open active conformation.
source: In the closed conformation, the N′ SH2 domain masks the catalytic domain rendering the enzyme inactive, whereas when the catalytic domain is free of the N′ SH2 domain, the protein remains in an open active conformation (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: An inactive SHP-1 protein provides high FRET efficiency due to YFP and CFP proximity.
source: Hence, an inactive SHP-1 protein provides high FRET efficiency due to YFP and CFP proximity, and an active SHP-1 protein demonstrates low FRET efficiency as SHP-1 is in an open conformation, distancing the two reporter proteins.
evidence: This is based on the principle of FRET biosensor design and established knowledge.

claim: An active SHP-1 protein demonstrates low FRET efficiency as SHP-1 is in an open conformation, distancing the two reporter proteins.
source: Hence, an inactive SHP-1 protein provides high FRET efficiency due to YFP and CFP proximity, and an active SHP-1 protein demonstrates low FRET efficiency as SHP-1 is in an open conformation, distancing the two reporter proteins.
evidence: This is based on the principle of FRET biosensor design and established knowledge.

claim: During initial inhibitory NK:721-Cw4 interactions (5 min), SHP-1 in NK cells displayed low synaptic FRET efficiency, indicating an open and active state (8.62% ± 1.8%).
source: FRET measurements demonstrated patterns similar to SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation profiles; during initial inhibitory NK:721-Cw4 interactions (5 min), SHP-1 in NK cells displayed low synaptic FRET efficiency, indicating an open and active state (8.62% ± 1.8%), shifting to high FRET efficiency after 20 min of synapse maturation (15.13% ± 1.9%, p=0.0300; Figure 2A and B, top two panels), indicating a closed and inhibited state.
evidence: This is supported by FRET microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: SHP-1 shifts to high FRET efficiency after 20 min of inhibitory synapse maturation (15.13% ± 1.9%, p=0.0300), indicating a closed and inhibited state.
source: FRET measurements demonstrated patterns similar to SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation profiles; during initial inhibitory NK:721-Cw4 interactions (5 min), SHP-1 in NK cells displayed low synaptic FRET efficiency, indicating an open and active state (8.62% ± 1.8%), shifting to high FRET efficiency after 20 min of synapse maturation (15.13% ± 1.9%, p=0.0300; Figure 2A and B, top two panels), indicating a closed and inhibited state.
evidence: This is supported by FRET microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: During activating interactions, SHP-1 in NK cells displayed highest synaptic FRET efficiency after 5 min (18.45% ± 1.9%, p=0.0003 comparing 5 min of activation to inhibition), indicating a closed and inhibited state.
source: During activating interactions, however, SHP-1 in NK cells displayed highest synaptic FRET efficiency after 5 min (18.45% ± 1.9%, p=0.0003 comparing 5 min of activation to inhibition), indicating a closed and inhibited state, while after 20 min of activation, a decrease was observed in SHP-1 FRET efficiency to similar levels as NK:721-Cw4 interactions after 5 min (8.15% ± 1.9%, p=0.006; Figure 2A and B, bottom two panels), indicating an open and active SHP-1 conformation (Matalon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by FRET microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: After 20 min of activation, a decrease was observed in SHP-1 FRET efficiency to similar levels as NK:721-Cw4 interactions after 5 min (8.15% ± 1.9%, p=0.006), indicating an open and active SHP-1 conformation.
source: During activating interactions, however, SHP-1 in NK cells displayed highest synaptic FRET efficiency after 5 min (18.45% ± 1.9%, p=0.0003 comparing 5 min of activation to inhibition), indicating a closed and inhibited state, while after 20 min of activation, a decrease was observed in SHP-1 FRET efficiency to similar levels as NK:721-Cw4 interactions after 5 min (8.15% ± 1.9%, p=0.006; Figure 2A and B, bottom two panels), indicating an open and active SHP-1 conformation (Matalon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by FRET microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B, with citation to prior work.

claim: NK cells are able to rapidly distinguish between activating and inhibitory target cells as measured by higher pSHP-1 S591 levels that were localized to synapses with K562, versus 721-Cw4 cells.
source: Strikingly, NK cells were able to rapidly distinguish between activating and inhibitory targets cells as measured by higher pSHP-1 S591 levels that were localized to synapses with K562, versus 721-Cw4 cells (Figure 3A, p=0.0074).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing differential pSHP-1 S591 localization in dual synapses shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PKC-θ is expressed predominantly in hematopoietic and muscle cells.
source: PKC-θ is expressed predominantly in hematopoietic and muscle cells (Osada et al., 1992; Baier et al., 1993), and was shown to play multiple roles in T cell activation (Hayashi and Altman, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PKC-θ was shown to play multiple roles in T cell activation.
source: PKC-θ is expressed predominantly in hematopoietic and muscle cells (Osada et al., 1992; Baier et al., 1993), and was shown to play multiple roles in T cell activation (Hayashi and Altman, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PKC-θ was suggested to participate in murine NK cell activity.
source: PKC-θ was suggested to participate in murine NK cell activity (Tassi et al., 2008; Aguiló et al., 2009; Anel et al., 2012; Merino et al., 2012); however, the mechanism by which it exerts this function remains unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TNF-α and IFN-γ secretion is defective in PKC-θ−/− mice.
source: It was shown that TNF-α and IFN-γ secretion is defective in PKC-θ−/− mice (Page et al., 2008), and this can contribute to defective recruitment of effector cells to the site of tumor development.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: No effect of PKC-θ deficiency was observed on IFN-γ secretion induced by IL-12, IL-18, or a combination of both cytokines.
source: In a different study (Tassi et al., 2008), no effect of PKC-θ deficiency was observed on IFN-γ secretion induced by IL-12, IL-18, or a combination of both cytokines.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PKC-θ localizes to the cytolytic NK synapse during early activation, following 5 and 10 min of activating target cell conjugation.
source: Early reports by Vyas et al. showed that PKC-θ localizes to the cytolytic NK synapse during early activation, that is, following 5 and 10 min of activating target cell conjugation, and relatively low PKC-θ polarization is observed following 10 min of non-cytolytic NK: target cell conjugates (Vyas et al., 2002a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Relatively low PKC-θ polarization is observed following 10 min of non-cytolytic NK: target cell conjugates.
source: Early reports by Vyas et al. showed that PKC-θ localizes to the cytolytic NK synapse during early activation, that is, following 5 and 10 min of activating target cell conjugation, and relatively low PKC-θ polarization is observed following 10 min of non-cytolytic NK: target cell conjugates (Vyas et al., 2002a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PKC-θ localization appeared dispersed at the early inhibitory NKIS and accumulated at the synapse after 20 min (p=0.0036).
source: PKC-θ localization appeared dispersed at the early inhibitory NKIS and accumulated at the synapse after 20 min (p=0.0036).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PKC-θ accumulation at the activating NKIS at the initial time point did not significantly decrease after 20 min (p=0.5068).
source: Furthermore, we observed PKC-θ accumulation at the activating NKIS at the initial time point, which did not significantly decrease after 20 min (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, p=0.5068).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significant silencing efficiency of PKC-θ was obtained in YTS-2DL1 cells (p=0.001).
source: Significant silencing efficiency was obtained in all experiments (p=0.001 and p=0.0135 for YTS and pNK-2DL1 cells, respectively) relative to cells transfected with nonspecific (NS) siRNA control (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data showing PKC-θ knockdown efficiency in Figure 4A.

claim: Significant silencing efficiency of PKC-θ was obtained in pNK-2DL1 cells (p=0.0135).
source: Significant silencing efficiency was obtained in all experiments (p=0.001 and p=0.0135 for YTS and pNK-2DL1 cells, respectively) relative to cells transfected with nonspecific (NS) siRNA control (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data showing PKC-θ knockdown efficiency in Figure 4C.

claim: A reduction in SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation levels was observed in YTS-2DL1 treated with PKC-θ siRNA as opposed to NS siRNA (by 2.5-fold ± 0.03, p=0.0072).
source: Though S591 phosphorylation was not completely eliminated, a reduction in SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation levels could be seen in YTS-2DL1 or pNK-2DL1 treated with PKC-θ siRNA as opposed to NS siRNA (by 2.5-fold ± 0.03, p=0.0072; by 1.7-fold ± 0.07, p=0.0113, respectively) (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A reduction in SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation levels was observed in pNK-2DL1 treated with PKC-θ siRNA as opposed to NS siRNA (by 1.7-fold ± 0.07, p=0.0113).
source: Though S591 phosphorylation was not completely eliminated, a reduction in SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation levels could be seen in YTS-2DL1 or pNK-2DL1 treated with PKC-θ siRNA as opposed to NS siRNA (by 2.5-fold ± 0.03, p=0.0072; by 1.7-fold ± 0.07, p=0.0113, respectively) (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Synaptic FRET efficiency was significantly reduced in YTS-2DL1 YFP-SHP-1-CFP cells pretreated with PKC-θ siRNA versus NS siRNA (18.5% ± 2.04% vs. 9.8% ± 1.7%, p=0.0025), suggesting that the SHP-1 in the silenced cells acquires the open conformation.
source: Synaptic FRET efficiency was significantly reduced in YTS-2DL1 YFP-SHP-1-CFP cells pretreated with PKC-θ siRNA versus NS siRNA (18.5% ± 2.04% vs. 9.8% ± 1.7%, p=0.0025), suggesting that the SHP-1 in the silenced cells acquires the open conformation (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by FRET microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: PKC-θ gene silencing reduced the FRET efficiency of YFP-SHP-1-CFP in the activating NKIS to similar FRET levels observed in YTS-2DL1 YFP-SHP-1-CFP cells pretreated with NS siRNA following inhibitory interactions (5.76% ± 1.6% vs. 9.8% ± 1.7%, p=0.2663).
source: Interestingly, PKC-θ gene silencing reduced the FRET efficiency of YFP-SHP-1-CFP in the activating NKIS to similar FRET levels observed in YTS-2DL1 YFP-SHP-1-CFP cells pretreated with NS siRNA following inhibitory interactions (5.76% ± 1.6% vs. 9.8% ± 1.7%, p=0.2663) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by FRET microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Direct catalytic activity of SHP-1 on the pNPP substrate was shown to be higher in cells treated with PKC-θ siRNA rather than in cells treated with NS siRNA (81% ± 3.3% vs. 65% ± 3% activity, p=0.0246).
source: Direct catalytic activity of SHP-1 on the pNPP substrate was shown to be higher in cells treated with PKC-θ siRNA rather than in cells treated with NS siRNA (81% ± 3.3% vs. 65% ± 3% activity, p=0.0246) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by PTP assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: SHP-1 dephosphorylates VAV1 as a mechanism of terminating NK cell activation.
source: SHP-1 was shown to dephosphorylate VAV1 as a mechanism of terminating NK cell activation (Stebbins et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: IB of pVAV1 (Y160) revealed an approximately twofold reduction in phosphorylation levels in activated YTS-2DL1 samples treated with PKC-θ siRNA in contrast to NS siRNA (p=0.0001).
source: IB (immunoblotted) of pVAV1 (Y160) revealed an approximately twofold reduction in phosphorylation levels in activated YTS-2DL1 samples treated with PKC-θ siRNA in contrast to NS siRNA (p=0.0001) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: pNK-2DL1 cells demonstrated a similar reduction in pVAV1 (Y160) phosphorylation levels subsequent to PKC-θ gene silencing (p=0.0192).
source: Similarly, pNK-2DL1 cells demonstrated a similar reduction in pVAV1 (Y160) phosphorylation levels subsequent to PKC-θ gene silencing (p=0.0192) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: pNK-2DL1 cells showed a 1.8-fold ± 0.2 reduction in pPLCγ1 levels (p=0.0032) when treated with PKC-θ siRNA.
source: In addition to VAV1, pNK-2DL1 cells showed a 1.8-fold ± 0.2 reduction in pPLCγ1 levels (p=0.0032) when treated with PKC-θ siRNA (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: YTS-2DL1 cells in which IP of PLCγ1 and IB of pPLCγ1 (Y783) revealed a reduction of 1.4-fold ± 0.04 in pPLCγ1 levels following PKC-θ gene silencing under activating interactions (p=0.0074).
source: A similar trend can be seen in YTS-2DL1 cells in which immunoprecipitation (IP) of PLCγ1 and IB of pPLCγ1 (Y783) revealed a reduction of 1.4-fold ± 0.04 in pPLCγ1 levels following PKC-θ gene silencing under activating interactions (p=0.0074) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: pVAV1 Y160 accumulation was observed during activating but not inhibitory NK cell interactions (p<0.0001).
source: As expected, pVAV1 Y160 accumulation was observed during activating but not inhibitory NK cell interactions (p<0.0001), and in accordance with our results, PKC-θ siRNA-treated NK cells had a 2 ± 0.2-fold reduction in pVAV1 recruitment to the activating NKIS (p<0.0001), indicating increased SHP-1 activity in the absence of PKC-θ under activating interactions (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PKC-θ siRNA-treated NK cells had a 2 ± 0.2-fold reduction in pVAV1 recruitment to the activating NKIS (p<0.0001), indicating increased SHP-1 activity in the absence of PKC-θ under activating interactions.
source: As expected, pVAV1 Y160 accumulation was observed during activating but not inhibitory NK cell interactions (p<0.0001), and in accordance with our results, PKC-θ siRNA-treated NK cells had a 2 ± 0.2-fold reduction in pVAV1 recruitment to the activating NKIS (p<0.0001), indicating increased SHP-1 activity in the absence of PKC-θ under activating interactions (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: No significant decrease in pVAV1 recruitment was observed in YTS-2DL1 SHP-1 S591D cells treated with either NS or PKC-θ siRNA under either activating or inhibitory interactions (p=0.9109 and p=0.9999, respectively).
source: No significant decrease in pVAV1 recruitment was observed, however, in YTS-2DL1 SHP-1 S591D cells treated with either NS or PKC-θ siRNA under either activating or inhibitory interactions (p=0.9109 and p=0.9999, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cells expressing SHP-1 S591D showed high levels of pPLCγ1 (Y783) accumulation at the NKIS, even though the NKIS was inhibitory, approximately three-fold higher compared to YTS-2DL1 cells expressing SHP-1 WT or SHP-1 S591A (p<0.0001).
source: Interestingly, cells expressing SHP-1 S591D showed high levels of pPLCγ1 (Y783) accumulation at the NKIS, even though the NKIS was inhibitory. These levels were approximately three-fold higher compared to YTS-2DL1 cells expressing SHP-1 WT or SHP-1 S591A (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Calcium flux levels were higher in activated vs. inhibited NK cells treated with NS siRNA.
source: As expected, calcium flux levels were higher in activated vs. inhibited NK cells treated with NS siRNA (black vs. blue curve, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by calcium flux measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claim: PKC-θ siRNA reversed the calcium flux trend, reducing calcium flux levels during NK cell activation near the levels obtained during NK cell inhibition.
source: However, PKC-θ siRNA reversed this trend, reducing calcium flux levels during NK cell activation near the levels obtained during NK cell inhibition (green vs. blue curve, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by calcium flux measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Target cell death was significantly reduced in YTS-2DL1 samples that were gene-silenced for PKC-θ under activating interactions (22% ± 3% vs. 42% ± 0.4%, p=0.0037).
source: Target cell death was significantly reduced in YTS-2DL1 samples that were gene-silenced for PKC-θ under activating interactions (22% ± 3% vs. 42% ± 0.4%, p=0.0037).
evidence: This is supported by Met release cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Activating target cells (Cw7) incubated with PKC-θ-silenced NK cells demonstrated lysis levels similar to those of inhibitory targets (Cw4) incubated with YTS-2DL1 cells treated with NS siRNA (22% ± 3% vs. 13% ± 2.7%, p=0.1015).
source: In fact, activating target cells (Cw7) incubated with PKC-θ-silenced NK cells demonstrated lysis levels similar to those of inhibitory targets (Cw4) incubated with YTS-2DL1 cells treated with NS siRNA (22% ± 3% vs. 13% ± 2.7%, p=0.1015).
evidence: This is supported by Met release cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: NK cells that were deficient in SHP-1 or both SHP-1 and PKC-θ displayed higher degranulation than WT cells (p=0.0127 and p=0.0001) and were not significantly affected by the presence or absence of PKC-θ (p=0.0603).
source: As can be seen in Figure 7D, NK cells that were deficient in SHP-1 or both SHP-1 and PKC-θ displayed higher degranulation than WT cells (p=0.0127 and p=0.0001) and were not significantly affected by the presence or absence of PKC-θ (p=0.0603).
evidence: This is supported by CD107a degranulation assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: PKC-θ knockdown inhibits the NK cell-mediated antitumor response against 721-Cw7 cells as demonstrated by reduced NK cell degranulation compared to YTS-2DL1 cells treated with NS siRNA (p=0.0040).
source: Furthermore, as shown in Figure 7E, PKC-θ knockdown also inhibits the NK cell-mediated antitumor response against 721-Cw7 cells as demonstrated by reduced NK cell degranulation compared to YTS-2DL1 cells treated with NS siRNA (p=0.0040).
evidence: This is supported by CD107a degranulation assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: YTS-2DL1 SHP-1 S591D and YTS-2DL1 SHP-1 KO cells treated with NS or PKC-θ siRNA demonstrated restored degranulation (p=0.04) against activating target cells, suggesting that antitumor responses were rescued by the absence of SHP-1 or the SHP-1 mutation at the PKC-θ phosphorylation site.
source: Additionally, YTS-2DL1 SHP-1 S591D and YTS-2DL1 SHP-1 KO cells treated with NS or PKC-θ siRNA demonstrated restored degranulation (p=0.04) against activating target cells, suggesting that antitumor responses were rescued by the absence of SHP-1 or the SHP-1 mutation at the PKC-θ phosphorylation site.
evidence: This is supported by CD107a degranulation assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Mice injected with YTS-2DL1 SHP-1-deficient/catalytically inactive cells that were treated with PKC-θ siRNA demonstrated slower tumor growth rates and smaller tumor volumes compared to mice injected with WT NK cells.
source: Indeed, mice injected with YTS-2DL1 SHP-1-deficient/catalytically inactive cells that were treated with PKC-θ siRNA demonstrated slower tumor growth rates and smaller tumor volumes compared to mice injected with WT NK cells (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 8.

claim: PKC-θ-silenced NK cells exhibited decreased antitumor activity toward activating target cells (721-Cw7).
source: As expected, PKC-θ-silenced NK cells exhibited decreased antitumor activity toward activating target cells (721-Cw7), while mice engrafted with YTS-2DL1 SHP-/- gene-silenced to PKC-θ exhibited a stronger antitumor response with lower tumor growth rates, suggesting that loss of SHP-1 activity restored the NK antitumor responses (p<0.0001, Figure 8D and E, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 8D and E.

claim: Mice engrafted with YTS-2DL1 SHP-/- gene-silenced to PKC-θ exhibited a stronger antitumor response with lower tumor growth rates, suggesting that loss of SHP-1 activity restored the NK antitumor responses (p<0.0001).
source: As expected, PKC-θ-silenced NK cells exhibited decreased antitumor activity toward activating target cells (721-Cw7), while mice engrafted with YTS-2DL1 SHP-/- gene-silenced to PKC-θ exhibited a stronger antitumor response with lower tumor growth rates, suggesting that loss of SHP-1 activity restored the NK antitumor responses (p<0.0001, Figure 8D and E, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 8D and E.

claim: SHP-1 plays a central role in the regulation of the NK cell activation threshold.
source: SHP-1 plays a central role in the regulation of the NK cell activation threshold (Stebbins et al., 2003; Lanier, 2005; Long, 2008; Matalon et al., 2016) and is critical for the NK cell education process (Viant et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SHP-1 is critical for the NK cell education process.
source: SHP-1 plays a central role in the regulation of the NK cell activation threshold (Stebbins et al., 2003; Lanier, 2005; Long, 2008; Matalon et al., 2016) and is critical for the NK cell education process (Viant et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Activation of SHP-1 and its homolog SHP-2 are the major mechanisms operating downstream to immune checkpoint receptors, such as PD-1, CTLA-4, BTLA, and LAG-3.
source: Importantly, activation of SHP-1 and its homolog SHP-2 (an additional critical inhibitory NK cell regulatory enzyme) (Purdy and Campbell, 2009) are the major mechanisms operating downstream to immune checkpoint receptors, such as PD-1, CTLA-4, BTLA, and LAG-3 (Lee et al., 1998; Watanabe et al., 2003; Sheppard et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Studies published on outcomes of SHP-1 C′ terminal serine phosphorylation in non-NK cell systems demonstrated contradicting results.
source: Studies published on outcomes of SHP-1 C′ terminal serine phosphorylation in non-NK cell systems demonstrated contradicting results (Li et al., 1995; Brumell et al., 1997; Jones et al., 2004; Poole and Jones, 2005; Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature showing conflicting findings.

claim: Phosphorylation of SHP-1 by PKC-θ during NK cell activation on serine 591 maintains heightened NK cell effector function by retaining the SHP-1 closed and inactive conformation.
source: Here, we demonstrate that phosphorylation of SHP-1 by PKC-θ during NK cell activation on serine 591 maintains heightened NK cell effector function by retaining the SHP-1 closed and inactive conformation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The PKC-θ:SHP-1 axis may play an important role in NK immune surveillance and tumor clearance.
source: Thus, the PKC-θ:SHP-1 axis may play an important role in NK immune surveillance and tumor clearance, a topic that has recently gained much attention in the immunotherapy field, especially in the context of adoptive cell transfer and genetically engineered NK cells (Dotta et al., 2007; Morandi et al., 2008; Ahern and Brennan, 2011; Jochems et al., 2016; Siegler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of SHP-1 during termination of the inhibitory NKIS may retain the activity of NK cells to subsequent targets.
source: Phosphorylation of SHP-1 during termination of the inhibitory NKIS may retain the activity of NK cells to subsequent targets, whereas its immediate phosphorylation at the activating NKIS maintains the NK cell lytic capacity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings about SHP-1 phosphorylation dynamics.

claim: Immediate phosphorylation of SHP-1 at the activating NKIS maintains the NK cell lytic capacity.
source: Phosphorylation of SHP-1 during termination of the inhibitory NKIS may retain the activity of NK cells to subsequent targets, whereas its immediate phosphorylation at the activating NKIS maintains the NK cell lytic capacity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings about SHP-1 phosphorylation dynamics.

claim: Mathematical modeling analysis in NK cells suggests that weak ligands for activating receptors (bearing partially phosphorylated ITAMs) can recruit SHP-1 and thereby increase the NK activation threshold.
source: Interestingly, mathematical modeling analysis in NK cells suggests that weak ligands for activating receptors (bearing partially phosphorylated ITAMs) can recruit SHP-1 and thereby increase the NK activation threshold, while under certain conditions (such as low concentration of SHP-1 and weak activating ligands) inhibitory receptors can aid in NK cell activation (Das, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature on mathematical modeling.

claim: Under certain conditions (such as low concentration of SHP-1 and weak activating ligands) inhibitory receptors can aid in NK cell activation.
source: Interestingly, mathematical modeling analysis in NK cells suggests that weak ligands for activating receptors (bearing partially phosphorylated ITAMs) can recruit SHP-1 and thereby increase the NK activation threshold, while under certain conditions (such as low concentration of SHP-1 and weak activating ligands) inhibitory receptors can aid in NK cell activation (Das, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature on mathematical modeling.

claim: PKC-θ is the only PKC isoform that was shown to accumulate at T cell and NKISs.
source: PKC-θ is the only PKC isoform that was shown to accumulate at T cell and NKISs (Monks et al., 1997; Merino et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In T cells, PKC-θ plays an important role in T cell activation and survival by activating several downstream pathways, including NF-kB and AP-1 as major targets.
source: In T cells, it is clear that PKC-θ plays an important role in T cell activation and survival by activating several downstream pathways, including NF-kB and AP-1 as major targets (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Clustering of PKC-θ at the NKIS amplifies murine NK cell activation and effector functions.
source: In addition, Merino et al. previously showed that clustering of PKC-θ at the NKIS amplifies murine NK cell activation and effector functions (Merino et al., 2012), but the mechanism by which it exerts this function and specifically in human cells remained mostly unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In human NK cells PKC-θ phosphorylates SHP-1 on S591, suppresses SHP-1 activity, and thereby increases NK cell activity.
source: Here, we demonstrate that in human NK cells PKC-θ phosphorylates SHP-1 on S591 (Figure 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suppresses SHP-1 activity, and thereby increases NK cell activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: PKC-θ appears to regulate SHP-1 activity during the late inhibitory synapse and through the full duration of activating NK:target cell interactions.
source: PKC-θ appears to regulate SHP-1 activity during the late inhibitory synapse and through the full duration of activating NK:target cell interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal dynamics of PKC-θ localization and SHP-1 phosphorylation shown in the data.

claim: Gene silencing of PKC-θ resulted in the closed SHP-1 conformation, implying that SHP-1 favors an open and active conformation in the absence of PKC-θ.
source: Indeed, gene silencing of PKC-θ resulted in the closed SHP-1 conformation (Figure 5), implying that SHP-1 favors an open and active conformation in the absence of PKC-θ.
evidence: This is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Absence of SHP-1 increased NK cell activity and decreased tumor progression, irrespective of PKC-θ expression.
source: These findings were strengthened through in vivo experiments, which demonstrated that absence of SHP-1 increased NK cell activity and decreased tumor progression, irrespective of PKC-θ expression, implying that PKC-θ indeed maintains NK cell activation through its regulation of SHP-1.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in Figure 8.

claim: PKC-θ also plays a role in NF-κB activation.
source: PKC-θ also plays a role in NF-κB activation as shown by Sun et al., 2000.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PKC-θ knockout could possibly affect NF-κB transcriptional activity, resulting in a reduced antitumor immune response.
source: Thus, PKC-θ knockout could possibly affect NF-κB transcriptional activity, resulting in a reduced antitumor immune response.
evidence: This is speculation based on known PKC-θ functions.

claim: A dynamic and coordinated balance between activating and inhibitory signaling cascades governs NK cell activation programs.
source: It seems that a dynamic and coordinated balance between activating and inhibitory signaling cascades governs NK cell activation programs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and established knowledge.

claim: NK cell tolerance or activation is modulated by signal strength of the target cells.
source: Das et al. proposed that NK cell tolerance or activation is modulated by signal strength of the target cells (Das, 2010), which is in line with the suggestion that NK cell regulation occurs through a balance of activating and inhibitory signals transmitted by membrane receptors recognizing potential ligands on the target cell surface (Lanier, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Deficiency or inhibition of PKC-θ could potentially decrease the severity of autoimmunity, allergy, and chronic inflammation.
source: Several studies show that deficiency or inhibition of PKC-θ could potentially decrease the severity of autoimmunity, allergy, and chronic inflammation.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Other serine/threonine kinases or isoforms such as PKC-θ may also be involved in SHP-1 phosphorylation.
source: It is possible that other serine/threonine kinases or isoforms such as PKC-θ may also be involved in this process (Jones et al., 2004).
evidence: This is speculation based on incomplete elimination of phosphorylation and prior literature.

claim: SHP-1 conformation and activity is dependent on the association to the cytoskeletal machinery and cytoskeletal dynamics.
source: We recently demonstrated that SHP-1 conformation and activity is dependent on the association to the cytoskeletal machinery and cytoskeletal dynamics (Matalon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work from the authors' group.

claim: Cross-talk between PKC-θ and SHP-1 may mediate actin:SHP-1 binding or disassociation, thereby regulating SHP-1 catalytic activity and conformation.
source: One possibility is that cross-talk between PKC-θ and SHP-1 mediates actin:SHP-1 binding or disassociation, thereby regulating SHP-1 catalytic activity and conformation.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: PKC-θ phosphorylates the Wiskott-Interacting Protein (WIP) in NK cells upon activation, and this facilitates recruitment of actin and myosin IIA to WIP and WASp for the formation of the multiprotein complex.
source: Furthermore, PKC-θ phosphorylates the Wiskott-Interacting Protein (WIP) in NK cells upon activation, and this facilitates recruitment of actin and myosin IIA to WIP and WASp for the formation of the multiprotein complex (Krzewski et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NKIS maintenance is highly regulated, and signaling events that lead to NK cell attachment to new target cells accelerate the detachment from previous targets.
source: It was recently demonstrated that NKIS maintenance is highly regulated, and signaling events that lead to NK cell attachment to new target cells accelerate the detachment from previous targets (Netter et al., 2017; Srpan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Highly regulated lytic granule convergence to the microtubule organizing center (MTOC) is crucial for NK cells to avoid bystander cell killing.
source: Furthermore, highly regulated lytic granule convergence to the microtubule organizing center (MTOC) is crucial for NK cells to avoid bystander cell killing (Hsu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation may enable rapid discrimination by NK cells between healthy and malignant targets, facilitating controlled and sequential killing in a heterogeneous environment.
source: We hypothesized that SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation may thus enable rapid discrimination by NK cells between healthy and malignant targets, facilitating controlled and sequential killing in a heterogeneous environment.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation is a regulated and directed event and may allow NK cells to locally regulate SHP-1 phosphorylation to enable the maintenance of multiple local activation states in a single cell.
source: Hence, SHP-1 S591 phosphorylation is a regulated and directed event and may allow NK cells to locally regulate SHP-1 phosphorylation to enable the maintenance of multiple local activation states in a single cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dual synapse data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cancer cells can express MHC-I and other inhibitory NK cell ligands.
source: Cancer cells can express MHC-I and other inhibitory NK cell ligands; thus, recruitment and activation of PKC-θ at the activating NKIS may limit SHP-1 association to ITIMs that could prevent tumor cell killing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer immune evasion.

claim: Recruitment and activation of PKC-θ at the activating NKIS may limit SHP-1 association to ITIMs that could prevent tumor cell killing.
source: Cancer cells can express MHC-I and other inhibitory NK cell ligands; thus, recruitment and activation of PKC-θ at the activating NKIS may limit SHP-1 association to ITIMs that could prevent tumor cell killing.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: S591 phosphorylation may not only affect the NK cell activation threshold, but also NK cell education, as SHP-1 was shown to be vital for regulating NK cell responsiveness to tumors.
source: It would be interesting to assess the effect of S591 phosphorylation on SHP-1:KIR ITIM association as this phosphorylation may not only affect the NK cell activation threshold, but also NK cell education, as SHP-1 was shown to be vital for regulating NK cell responsiveness to tumors (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions, supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NK cells are implicated in autoimmune disorders such as multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and type I diabetes.
source: Due to the fact that NK cells are also implicated in autoimmune disorders such as multiple sclerosis (Morandi et al., 2008), rheumatoid arthritis (Ahern and Brennan, 2011), and type I diabetes (Dotta et al., 2007), deregulation of SHP-1 activity may be a factor affecting normal NK cell functions against healthy cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Deregulation of SHP-1 activity may be a factor affecting normal NK cell functions against healthy cells.
source: Due to the fact that NK cells are also implicated in autoimmune disorders such as multiple sclerosis (Morandi et al., 2008), rheumatoid arthritis (Ahern and Brennan, 2011), and type I diabetes (Dotta et al., 2007), deregulation of SHP-1 activity may be a factor affecting normal NK cell functions against healthy cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the role of NK cells in autoimmunity.

claim: SHP-1 serves as an important regulator that impacts cell proliferation and survival.
source: SHP-1 was also shown to serve as an important regulator that impacts cell proliferation and survival (Chong and Maiese, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Some studies examined SHP-1's role in tumor transformation.
source: Some studies examined its role in tumor transformation (Wu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Lower abundance of SHP-1 in NK cells enhances their tumoricidal capacity.
source: Furthermore, it was recently shown that lower abundance of SHP-1 in NK cells enhances their tumoricidal capacity (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Abrogation of SHP-1 activity in engineered NK cells can have enhanced benefits for NK-based immunotherapeutic approaches.
source: We recently demonstrated that abrogation of SHP-1 activity in engineered NK cells can have enhanced benefits for NK-based immunotherapeutic approaches (Ben-Shmuel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work from the authors' group.
